question.knowledge_point: Evaluating an Improper Integral by Applying the Basic Result
question.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the following result:

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}z=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(z)+C
$$

We proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to -\infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{-1}\frac{8}{1+{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}z & =8\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{-1}\frac{1}{1+{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}z \\  & =8\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(z)]_{a}^{-1} \\  & =8\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(-1)-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(a)] \\  & =8\cdot (-\frac{\pi }{4}-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(a)])\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall the end behavior of the function $y=\operatorname{arctan}⁡x,$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡x]=-\frac{\pi }{2}$

- ${lim}_{x\to \infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡x]=\frac{\pi }{2}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14039465/assets/27ec65761e5119be666e69b67b2fa2fcb7b4f3665ddc41faddd6c136d5c955b1.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{-1}\frac{8}{1+{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}z & =8\cdot (-\frac{\pi }{4}-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(a)]) \\  & =8\cdot (-\frac{\pi }{4}-(-\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =8\cdot (\frac{\pi }{2}-\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Improper Integrals Involving Arctangent Using the First Result
question.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the following result:

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+(kx)^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{k}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(kx)+C
$$

We proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to -\infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{-\sqrt{3}/2}\frac{6}{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =6\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{-\sqrt{3}/2}\frac{1}{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =6\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{-\sqrt{3}/2}\frac{1}{1+(2x)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =6\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(2x)]}_{a}^{-\sqrt{3}/2} \\  & =3\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(-\sqrt{3})-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(2a)] \\  & =3\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }(-\frac{\pi }{3}-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(2a)) \\  & =-\pi -3\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(2a)].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall the end behavior of the function $y=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(2x),$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(2x)]=-\frac{\pi }{2}$

- ${lim}_{x\to \infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(2x)]=\frac{\pi }{2}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14039465/assets/382ca84f05af04af9c9b2c837d549a09b695574781f12bc67b8438b95b5f5d75.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{-\sqrt{3}/2}\frac{1}{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =-\pi -3\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(2a)] \\  & =-\pi -3\cdot (-\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =-\pi +\frac{3\pi }{2} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Improper Integrals Involving Arctangent Using the Second Result
question.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the following result:

$$
\int \frac{1}{{k}^{2}+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{k}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{k})+C
$$

We proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to \infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{2}{{z}^{2}+9}\,\text{d}z & =2\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}\frac{1}{{z}^{2}+9}\,\text{d}z \\  & =2\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}\frac{1}{{z}^{2}+{3}^{2}}\,\text{d}z \\  & =2\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{z}{3})]}_{0}^{a} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{a}{3})-\operatorname{arctan}⁡0) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{a}{3})]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall the end behavior of the function $y=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{3}),$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{3})]=-\frac{\pi }{2}$

- ${lim}_{x\to \infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{3})]=\frac{\pi }{2}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14039465/assets/2465f099a94aa966dbf33eb89aa00973e692fa97c887a9b79baff8260f5d31cd.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{2}{{z}^{2}+9}\,\text{d}z & =\frac{2}{3}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{a}{3})] \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\cdot \frac{\pi }{2} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Improper Integrals Involving Arctangent Using the Second Result
question.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the following result:

$$
\int \frac{1}{{k}^{2}+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{k}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{k})+C
$$

We proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to -\infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{1}\frac{1}{{u}^{2}+3}\,\text{d}u & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{1}\frac{1}{{u}^{2}+3}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{1}\frac{1}{{u}^{2}+{(\sqrt{3})}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\cdot \operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{u}{\sqrt{3}})]}_{a}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{a}{\sqrt{3}})] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }[\frac{\pi }{6}-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{a}{\sqrt{3}})] \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6\sqrt{3}}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{a}{\sqrt{3}})].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall the end behavior of the function $y=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}}),$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}})]=-\frac{\pi }{2}$

- ${lim}_{x\to \infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}})]=\frac{\pi }{2}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14039465/assets/11c74897fe914599a78c5997767bad83d13ddfb1e35ee66622d8880743688bad.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{1}\frac{1}{{u}^{2}+3}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{\pi }{6\sqrt{3}}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{a}{\sqrt{3}})] \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6\sqrt{3}}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\cdot (-\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\frac{2\pi }{3\sqrt{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Calculating Improper Integrals Involving Arctangent Using Substitution
question.worked_solution:
First, we substitute $u={e}^{x}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}={e}^{x}\,⟹\,\text{d}u={e}^{x}\text{d}x.
$$

Since $u\to \infty $ when $x\to \infty ,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u={e}^{x}$ is as follows:

| $x$ | $0$ | $\infty $ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $\infty $ |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{{e}^{x}}{1+3{e}^{2x}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{1+3{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to \infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{{e}^{x}}{1+3{e}^{2x}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{1+3{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{a}\frac{1}{1+3{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{[\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\cdot \operatorname{arctan}⁡(\sqrt{3}u)]}_{1}^{a} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\sqrt{3}u)]}_{1}^{a} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\sqrt{3}a)-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\sqrt{3})] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\cdot ({lim}_{a\to \infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\sqrt{3}a)]-\frac{\pi }{3})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, recall the end behavior of the function $y=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\sqrt{3}x),$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\sqrt{3}x)]=-\frac{\pi }{2}$

- ${lim}_{x\to \infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\sqrt{3}x)]=\frac{\pi }{2}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14039465/assets/f55b37b456a6ab60c495c64be5f7afe510dc0889890ed2a070b371f9bbe69c1a.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{{e}^{x}}{1+3{e}^{2x}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\cdot ({lim}_{a\to \infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\sqrt{3}a)]-\frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\cdot (\frac{\pi }{2}-\frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\cdot \frac{\pi }{6} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}\pi }{18}.\end{aligned}
$$
